generalKnowledge.what is a neutron star:
### Neutron Stars

A **neutron star** is the collapsed core of a massive star (8–20 solar masses) that exploded as a **supernova**. It is one of the densest objects in the universe.

[COSMIC_CARD: formula: ρ ≈ 4 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³ | result: ~1.4 solar masses in ~10 km diameter | style: indigo]

**Extreme properties:**
- Diameter: ~10–20 km (the size of a city)
- Mass: 1.4–3 solar masses
- Density: a teaspoon weighs ~100 million tonnes — denser than an atomic nucleus
- Surface gravity: ~2 × 10¹¹ m/s² (20 billion times Earth's gravity)
- Composed almost entirely of **neutrons** (electrons and protons forced together under immense pressure)

**Pulsars:**
Highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation. Detected as regular pulses — some rotate 700 times per second (millisecond pulsars). Used as cosmic clocks in pulsar timing arrays to detect gravitational waves.

**Magnetars:**
Neutron stars with extraordinarily strong magnetic fields (~10¹⁵ gauss, vs Earth's 0.5 gauss). Emit intense bursts of X-rays and gamma rays.

**Formation:** Core collapse during supernova; if the remnant exceeds ~3 solar masses, gravity overcomes neutron degeneracy pressure and it becomes a black hole instead.
generalKnowledge.what is the big bang:
### The Big Bang

The **Big Bang** is the prevailing cosmological model for the origin and evolution of the universe — describing how the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state approximately **13.8 billion years ago**.

[COSMIC_CARD: formula: t₀ ≈ 13.787 × 10⁹ years | result: Age of Universe | style: indigo]

**Timeline of the early universe:**
- **t = 0:** Singularity — all matter/energy/space compressed to a point (physics breaks down here)
- **t = 10⁻³⁶ s:** **Cosmic Inflation** — exponential expansion of space by factor ~10²⁶ in ~10⁻³² seconds
- **t = 3 minutes:** Nucleosynthesis — protons and neutrons fuse into hydrogen and helium nuclei
- **t = 380,000 years:** Recombination — electrons combine with nuclei; universe becomes transparent; **Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)** released
- **t = 180 million years:** First stars ignite
- **t = 13.8 Gyr:** Present day

**Evidence:**
- **CMB** — uniform 2.725 K glow from all directions (COBE, WMAP, Planck satellites)
- **Hubble's Law** — galaxies recede at speeds proportional to distance (universe is expanding)
- **Primordial nucleosynthesis** — observed hydrogen/helium ratio (~75%/25%) matches predictions

**Observable universe diameter:** ~93 billion light-years (larger than 13.8 Gly due to expansion).
generalKnowledge.how far is mars:
### Distance to Mars

The distance between Earth and Mars varies greatly due to both planets' elliptical orbits.

[COSMIC_CARD: formula: d_avg ≈ 225 million km | result: ~12.5 light-minutes average | style: indigo]

**Distance ranges:**
- **Minimum (opposition, favorable):** ~54.6 million km (~3 light-minutes) — closest approach
- **Average:** ~225 million km (~12.5 light-minutes)
- **Maximum (opposite sides of Sun):** ~401 million km (~22 light-minutes)

**Travel time to Mars:**
- **Light/radio signals:** 3–22 minutes one-way (6–44 min round-trip communication delay)
- **Spacecraft (Hohmann transfer orbit):** **7–9 months** using current propulsion
- **Fastest mission so far:** Mars Odyssey — ~200 days
- **With nuclear propulsion (theoretical):** ~3–4 months
- **With fusion drives (future):** potentially 6–8 weeks

**Opposition:**
Every ~26 months, Earth and Mars align on the same side of the Sun — optimal launch windows. The 2003 opposition was the closest in ~60,000 years (55.76 million km).

**Mars missions:** NASA's Perseverance rover (landed 2021), China's Zhurong (2021), and ESA/Roscosmos Trace Gas Orbiter are currently active.
generalKnowledge.what is the james webb telescope:
### James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)

JWST is NASA's flagship space observatory, launched December 25, 2021, and operational since July 2022 — the most powerful space telescope ever built.

[COSMIC_CARD: formula: λ = 0.6–28.5 μm (infrared) | result: Sees farther back in time than Hubble | style: indigo]

**Key specifications:**
- **Primary mirror:** 6.5 meters diameter (18 gold-coated hexagonal beryllium segments)
- **Wavelength:** Near-infrared to mid-infrared (0.6–28.5 μm)
- **Location:** **L2 Lagrange point** — 1.5 million km from Earth (sun-Earth-telescope aligned)
- **Sunshield:** 5 layers of kapton film (tennis court–sized); keeps telescope at −233°C
- **Cost:** ~$10 billion (joint NASA/ESA/CSA)

**Vs Hubble:**
- Mirror: 6.5 m vs Hubble's 2.4 m (6× collecting area)
- Infrared vs optical/UV — sees through dust clouds invisible to Hubble
- L2 orbit vs low Earth orbit — no atmospheric interference, better thermal stability

**Discoveries and capabilities:**
- Observed galaxies from **<400 million years after the Big Bang** — the earliest ever seen
- Detailed atmospheres of exoplanets via transmission spectroscopy
- Resolved star-forming regions inside dense nebulae (Carina Nebula, Pillars of Creation in new detail)
- Confirmed and refined Hubble constant measurements (contributing to the "Hubble tension" debate)
- Detected carbon dioxide, water, and organic molecules in exoplanet atmospheres
generalKnowledge.tell me about lions:
### Lion (*Panthera leo*)

The lion is the **second-largest wild cat** in the world, native to sub-Saharan Africa and a small population in India's Gir Forest.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** Males 180–230 kg; females 120–182 kg
- **Speed:** Up to **80 km/h (50 mph)** in short bursts
- **Lifespan:** 10–14 years (wild); up to 20 in captivity
- **Social:** Lions are the **only truly social cats** — they live in groups called **prides** (2–40 individuals)

**Pride structure:**
- 1–4 adult males, 4–12 females, and their cubs
- Females do ~90% of hunting, primarily at night
- Males defend territory and cubs from rival prides and hyenas

**Hunting & Diet:**
- Apex predator; prey includes zebra, wildebeest, buffalo, warthog
- Cooperative hunters — females encircle prey using coordinated ambush
- A single lion eats ~7 kg of meat per day on average

**Conservation:**
- Listed as **Vulnerable** on the IUCN Red List
- Population declined ~43% over 21 years (estimated 20,000–25,000 remain)
- Threats: habitat loss, prey depletion, human-wildlife conflict, trophy hunting
generalKnowledge.tell me about tigers:
### Tiger (*Panthera tigris*)

The tiger is the **largest wild cat** in the world and one of the most iconic apex predators on Earth.

**Subspecies (living):**
- **Bengal tiger** — most common (~2,500); India, Bangladesh, Nepal
- **Amur (Siberian) tiger** — largest subspecies; Russian Far East (~500)
- **Sumatran tiger** — smallest; critically endangered (~400)
- **Malayan, Indochinese, South China** — all endangered or critically so

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 90–310 kg depending on subspecies
- **Length:** up to 3.9 m (Amur tiger)
- **Speed:** ~50–65 km/h in short sprints
- **Lifespan:** 10–15 years wild; up to 25 in captivity
- **Stripe pattern:** unique to each individual — like a fingerprint

**Behavior:**
- Solitary and territorial — males hold 60–100 km² ranges
- Excellent swimmers; often cool off in rivers and lakes
- Stalk prey (deer, wild boar, gaur) using camouflage, pounce from close range
- Crepuscular — most active at dawn and dusk

**Conservation:**
- **Endangered** — ~3,900 tigers remain in the wild (down from 100,000 in 1900)
- Protected under CITES Appendix I; international trade banned
- TX2 goal: double wild tigers by 2022 — achieved in India (3,000+ in 2023)
generalKnowledge.tell me about wolves:
### Gray Wolf (*Canis lupus*)

The gray wolf is the **largest wild canid** and the ancestor of all domestic dog breeds.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 23–80 kg; males larger than females
- **Speed:** 50–60 km/h sustained; can travel 50–80 km per day
- **Lifespan:** 6–8 years wild; up to 13 in captivity
- **Range:** Widest natural range of any large land mammal — North America, Europe, Asia

**Pack dynamics:**
- Packs of 2–36 individuals led by an **alpha pair** (breeding male and female)
- Complex social hierarchy; communication through howls, body posture, and scent marking
- Howls can carry **10+ km** and serve for territory marking and pack coordination
- Cooperative hunting allows wolves to take prey 10× their own size (moose, elk, bison)

**Ecological role:**
- **Keystone predator** — regulates prey populations, shaping entire ecosystems
- **Yellowstone reintroduction (1995):** Adding 41 wolves triggered a **trophic cascade**:
  - Elk behavior changed → overgrazing stopped → willows and aspen recovered → rivers stabilized
  - Beaver populations increased → wetland habitats improved

**Conservation:**
- Extirpated from most of the US in the 20th century via hunting campaigns
- Reintroduced in Yellowstone, Idaho, and parts of Europe with mixed success
- Gray wolf: **Least Concern** globally but locally endangered in many regions
generalKnowledge.tell me about sharks:
### Shark Facts

Sharks are cartilaginous fish that have existed **450+ million years** — surviving all five mass extinctions.

- **~500 species** ranging from 17 cm (dwarf lanternshark) to 18 m (whale shark)
- **Great White:** Up to 6 m, 2,000 kg; apex predator; Vulnerable (~3,500 remain)
- **Whale Shark:** Largest fish on Earth; filter feeder; Endangered
- **Hammerhead:** 360° vision; electroreceptors detect buried prey
- **Biology:** Cartilage skeleton; 30,000+ teeth in a lifetime; ampullae of Lorenzini detect electric fields
- **Reproduction:** Diverse strategies — egg-laying, live birth, ovoviviparous

For full shark facts → ask **'tell me about sharks'** or **'tell me about hammerhead sharks'**
generalKnowledge.tell me about elephants:
### Elephants

Elephants are the **largest land animals on Earth** and among the most intelligent mammals.

**Three species:**
- **African Bush Elephant** — largest; up to 7,500 kg, 4 m tall at shoulder
- **African Forest Elephant** — smaller; rainforest dweller; genetically distinct
- **Asian Elephant** — smaller ears, more rounded back; found across South and SE Asia

**Key facts:**
- **Lifespan:** 60–70 years
- **Pregnancy:** **22 months** — the longest gestation of any land mammal
- **Brain:** Largest of any land animal at ~5 kg; ~3× the size of a human brain
- **Trunk:** Contains over **40,000 muscles**; used for breathing, smelling, drinking, grasping
- **Teeth:** 6 sets of molars over a lifetime; when the last set wears out, the elephant dies (can no longer eat)

**Intelligence & behavior:**
- **Self-aware** — recognize themselves in mirrors (one of very few animals to do so)
- Exhibit **grief** — known to return to bones of deceased family members and touch them with their trunks
- **Empathy** — comfort distressed herd members; "rescue" stuck or injured animals
- Use tools: modify branches to swat flies, scratch themselves
- Long-term memory: remember individuals and locations for decades

**Communication:**
- Infrasound calls below 20 Hz travel through the ground and are detected by feet — over 10 km range

**Conservation:**
- African elephant: **Vulnerable** to **Endangered**; ~415,000 remain (down from ~5 million in 1930)
- Primary threats: poaching for ivory, habitat loss and fragmentation
generalKnowledge.tell me about dolphins:
### Dolphins

Dolphins are highly intelligent **marine mammals** in the family Delphinidae — not fish, but air-breathing cetaceans closely related to whales.

**Key species:**
- **Bottlenose Dolphin** (*Tursiops truncatus*) — most studied; 190–650 kg, up to 4 m
- **Common Dolphin** — fastest cetacean at ~60 km/h; forms mega-pods of thousands
- **Orca (Killer Whale)** — largest dolphin; up to 6,000 kg; apex predator
- **Spinner Dolphin** — known for acrobatic spinning leaps

**Intelligence:**
- **Self-aware** — pass the mirror test
- Use **signature whistles** (unique to each individual — like a name) to identify themselves and others
- Demonstrate cultural learning: behaviors spread through social groups, not just genes
- Problem-solving: use sponges as nose guards while foraging on the seafloor (tool use)
- Dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia taught their calves this sponging behavior — one of the best examples of animal culture

**Echolocation:**
- Emit clicks up to **200,000 Hz** (well beyond human hearing)
- Bounced echoes map 3D environment, detect fish inside sand, and identify objects by shape
- Resolution fine enough to detect a golf ball at 75 m distance

**Social structure:**
- Live in fluid fission-fusion societies
- Form **alliances** — male dolphins cooperate in coalitions to compete for females
- Play, surf waves, and engage in non-reproductive sexual behavior

**Threats:** Bycatch, ocean noise pollution, habitat degradation, hunting (Taiji, Japan drives)
generalKnowledge.tell me about eagles:
### Eagles

Eagles are large **birds of prey** (raptors) in the family Accipitridae — apex aerial predators known for their power, size, and exceptional eyesight.

**Key species:**

**Bald Eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*):**
- National symbol of the United States
- Wingspan: up to 2.4 m; weight: 3–6.3 kg
- Recovers from near-extinction (417 pairs in 1963 → 10,000+ pairs today)
- Conservation success story — removed from endangered species list in 2007

**Golden Eagle (*Aquila chrysaetos*):**
- Most widely distributed eagle; found across Northern Hemisphere
- Fastest in level flight: ~240 km/h in a stoop (dive)
- Hunts rabbits, ground squirrels, prairie dogs; can take lambs and foxes

**Philippine Eagle (*Pithecophaga jefferyi*):**
- World's largest eagle by length and wingspan (up to 2.2 m span, 8 kg)
- National bird of the Philippines; **Critically Endangered** (~800 remain)
- Primary prey: monkeys, flying lemurs, large lizards

**Vision:**
- Eagles see **4–8× more sharply** than humans — can spot a rabbit from 3.2 km
- Two foveas (vs humans' one) for forward and lateral focus simultaneously
- UV vision helps detect rodent urine trails

**Flight:**
- Hollow bones make up only ~5% of body weight
- Lock-in tendons allow effortless gripping while sleeping on perches
- Thermal soaring — ride rising hot air columns for hours without flapping
generalKnowledge.tell me about octopuses:
### Octopus

Octopuses are **cephalopod mollusks** — soft-bodied, eight-armed marine invertebrates, widely regarded as the **most intelligent invertebrates on Earth**.

**Key facts:**
- ~300 known species; most live 1–2 years (short lifespan limits how much intelligence can evolve — yet their cognition remains remarkable)
- **3 hearts:** two pump blood to gills; one pumps it to the body
- **Blue blood:** contains hemocyanin (copper-based) instead of hemoglobin (iron-based)
- **Chromatophores:** thousands of pigment cells allow near-instant color/texture camouflage — despite being colorblind!

**Intelligence:**
- Distributed nervous system: **2/3 of neurons are in the 8 arms** — each arm can act semi-independently
- Learn by observation (watch and mimic other octopuses)
- Escape from tanks, navigate mazes, unscrew jars, use coconut shells as portable shelters (tool use)
- Play behavior: toss objects repeatedly in the water for no apparent reward
- Individual personalities documented in lab settings

**Defense:**
- Jet propulsion: expel water forcefully for rapid escape
- Ink cloud: disrupts predator's vision and impairs their sense of smell
- Autotomy: can detach an arm to distract a predator; arm regenerates
- Mimic octopus: impersonates 15+ other species (lionfish, flatfish, sea snakes)

**Reproduction:**
- Female lays 50,000–400,000 eggs; guards them obsessively for months, stopping eating
- Dies shortly after eggs hatch; males die after mating
generalKnowledge.tell me about gorillas:
### Gorilla

Gorillas are the **largest living primates** and our closest relatives after chimpanzees and bonobos — sharing ~98.3% of human DNA.

**Two species, four subspecies:**
- **Western Lowland Gorilla** — most numerous; found in Central/West Africa
- **Eastern Lowland Gorilla** — largest subspecies; critically endangered
- **Mountain Gorilla** — famous from Dian Fossey's work; ~1,000 remain
- **Cross River Gorilla** — rarest great ape; ~200–300 remain

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** Males (silverbacks) 140–270 kg; females 68–113 kg
- **Standing height:** up to 1.8 m
- **Strength:** estimated 4–10× stronger than an adult human
- **Lifespan:** 35–40 years wild; up to 50 in captivity
- **Diet:** Primarily herbivorous — leaves, stems, fruit, bark; occasionally insects

**Intelligence & behavior:**
- **Sign language:** Koko (1971–2018) learned over 1,000 American Sign Language signs and understood ~2,000 English words
- Tool use: use sticks to gauge water depth, leaves as rain protection
- **Silverback** leads a troop of 5–30; mediates conflicts, decides movement
- Gorillas build fresh **sleeping nests** every night in trees or on ground
- Chest beating: communication signal, not necessarily aggression

**Conservation:**
- All subspecies **Critically Endangered** except Western Lowland (Endangered)
- Mountain gorilla population has grown from 620 (2008) to ~1,000 today — a rare conservation success
generalKnowledge.tell me about cheetahs:
### Cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*)

The cheetah is the **fastest land animal on Earth** — a slender, aerodynamically built cat specialized for explosive speed.

**Speed:**
- Top speed: **112–120 km/h (70–75 mph)** over 200–300 m
- Acceleration: 0 to 96 km/h in ~3 seconds — faster than most sports cars
- Stride: up to 7–8 meters per stride at full speed; feet airborne ~50% of the time
- After a chase, must rest 15–30 minutes to lower body temperature before eating

**Key biology:**
- **Semi-retractable claws** — unlike other big cats, claws provide traction like cleats (not fully retracted)
- **Enlarged nasal passages, heart, and lungs** for rapid oxygen intake
- **Flexible spine** acts like a spring — dramatically increases stride length
- **Tear marks** (black lines from eye to mouth) — reduce sun glare, improve focus
- **Smallest of the big cats** — 21–72 kg; can't roar (chirps, purrs, yelps instead)

**Hunting:**
- Primarily diurnal (hunts by day) to avoid competition with lions and leopards
- Uses exceptional eyesight to spot prey from 5 km; relies on vision, not smell
- Success rate: ~50% (higher than lions ~25%)
- Kills with suffocating throat bite; often stolen by lions, hyenas, leopards

**Conservation:**
- **Vulnerable** — ~7,000 remain in the wild (down from 100,000 in 1900)
- Only ~50 remain in Iran (Asiatic subspecies — Critically Endangered)
- Cannot breed reliably in captivity; low genetic diversity from ancient bottleneck
generalKnowledge.tell me about penguins:
### Penguins

Penguins are **flightless seabirds** that exchanged aerial flight for extraordinary underwater agility — living exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere.

**18 species, from tiny to giant:**
- **Little Blue Penguin** — smallest; 33 cm, 1 kg; found in Australia and New Zealand
- **Emperor Penguin** — largest; 1.2 m, up to 46 kg; only animal to breed on Antarctic ice in winter
- **African Penguin** — only African species; endangered
- **Galápagos Penguin** — northernmost species; only one that lives near the equator

**Emperor Penguin breeding (most extreme):**
- Breeds in **Antarctic winter** (−60°C winds)
- Female lays one egg then returns to sea; male balances egg on feet, fasting for **65 days**
- 5,000+ males huddle together, rotating to share warmth — core of huddle reaches 37°C
- Lose 45% of body weight during fast

**Swimming:**
- Wings evolved into stiff flippers — cannot fly but swim up to **36 km/h**
- Emperor penguins dive to **565 m** depth; hold breath for **22 minutes**
- Double-layer waterproof feathers trap air for insulation (400 feathers per cm²)

**Social life:**
- Monogamous pairs; recognize each other and their chicks by unique calls
- Rookeries can hold **600,000 birds** (Adélie penguins)

**Conservation:**
- 8 of 18 species threatened; climate change shrinking Antarctic ice and fish stocks
generalKnowledge.tell me about polar bears:
### Polar Bear (*Ursus maritimus*)

The polar bear is the **world's largest land predator** and the apex predator of the Arctic — technically classified as a marine mammal.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** Males 400–700 kg; females 150–250 kg
- **Height:** Up to 3.5 m standing on hind legs
- **Speed:** Up to 40 km/h on land; excellent swimmer (6–10 km/h, documented 320 km+ swims)
- **Lifespan:** 25–30 years in the wild

**Arctic adaptations:**
- **Fur:** Appears white (actually transparent and hollow); reflects visible light; absorbs UV
- **Skin:** Black — maximizes heat absorption from UV light
- **Fat layer:** Up to 11 cm thick for insulation
- **Large paws:** Up to 30 cm wide, act as snowshoes and paddles; non-slip textured soles
- **Nose:** Can detect seals through 1 m of ice and snow from 1 km away
- **Semi-hibernation:** Pregnant females den in snow; body temperature only drops a few degrees (unlike true hibernators)

**Diet:**
- Almost exclusively **ringed seals** and bearded seals
- Primary hunting technique: **still hunting** — waiting motionless at breathing holes
- Can fast for 8+ months (living off fat reserves)

**Conservation:**
- **Vulnerable** — ~26,000 remain
- Entirely dependent on sea ice for hunting; Arctic sea ice declining ~13% per decade
- IUCN projects 30% population decline by 2050 under current warming trajectories
generalKnowledge.tell me about bees:
### Bees

Bees are **flying insects** in the order Hymenoptera, critical pollinators that directly support ~1/3 of the world's food supply.

**~20,000 known species** — most are solitary (only ~250 are bumblebees/honeybees).

**Honeybee (*Apis mellifera*) colony:**
- **Queen** — sole egg-layer; lives 2–5 years; lays up to 2,000 eggs/day
- **Workers** — sterile females; 20,000–80,000 per hive; live 6 weeks in summer
- **Drones** — males; only role is mating with queens; die after mating

**Honeybee biology:**
- Communicate via the **waggle dance** — figure-8 movement encodes direction (relative to sun) and distance of food sources
- Produce honey: nectar collected, partially digested, evaporated to ~17% water content
- **Beeswax:** Secreted from abdominal glands; used to build honeycomb (hexagonal cells — optimal geometry for maximum storage with minimum wax)
- One hive produces ~30–100 lbs of honey per year
- A honeybee visits 50–100 flowers per trip; makes **1/12 teaspoon of honey** in its lifetime

**Sting:**
- Worker honeybee stinger is barbed — remains in skin, pulling out the venom sac; bee dies
- Queen's stinger is smooth — can sting repeatedly
- Bumblebees and solitary bees can also sting repeatedly

**Pollination value:**
- Pollinators contribute ~$235 billion/year to global agriculture
- **Colony Collapse Disorder (CCD):** Mysterious die-offs since 2006; causes: pesticides (neonicotinoids), Varroa mites, habitat loss, pathogens
generalKnowledge.tell me about komodo dragons:
### Komodo Dragon (*Varanus komodoensis*)

The Komodo dragon is the **world's largest living lizard** — an apex predator native to a handful of Indonesian islands.

**Key facts:**
- **Length:** Up to 3 m; **Weight:** Up to 70 kg (males); females ~45 kg
- **Lifespan:** Up to 30 years
- **Habitat:** Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Motang islands — total range: ~1,000 km²
- **Listed:** Endangered — ~1,400 remain in the wild

**Hunting & Venom:**
- Once thought to kill via bacteria-laden bites; research (2009) proved they have **dual venom glands** between their teeth
- Venom prevents blood clotting (anticoagulant) and lowers blood pressure — causing shock and massive blood loss
- Forked tongue flicks 60× per minute to sample air; Jacobson's organ detects prey from **10 km away**
- Prey: deer, pigs, water buffalo, goats — will wait weeks after a bite for prey to weaken

**Physiology:**
- Can run at **20 km/h** in short bursts; excellent swimmers
- Serrated teeth continuously replaced; 60 teeth at any time
- Can eat **80% of their body weight** in a single meal
- 5-chambered heart (intermediate between reptile and mammal)

**Reproduction:**
- **Parthenogenesis:** Females can reproduce without males — virgin births documented; offspring are always male
- Eggs incubate for 7–8 months; hatchlings immediately live in trees to avoid cannibalism by adults
generalKnowledge.types of animals:
### The Animal Kingdom

Animals belong to the kingdom **Animalia** — multicellular, eukaryotic organisms that consume organic matter for energy.

**Major groups (Phyla):**

**Vertebrates (~65,000 species):**
| Class | Examples | Key trait |
|-------|---------|----------|
| Mammals | Humans, whales, bats | Warm-blooded, hair, nurse young with milk |
| Birds | Eagles, penguins, parrots | Warm-blooded, feathers, beaks |
| Reptiles | Crocodiles, snakes, lizards | Scales, ectothermic (cold-blooded) |
| Amphibians | Frogs, salamanders | Permeable skin, aquatic larvae |
| Fish | Sharks, tuna, salmon | Gills, fins; most ancient vertebrates |

**Invertebrates (~1.3 million species):**
| Group | Examples | Key trait |
|-------|---------|----------|
| Insects | Bees, beetles, ants | 6 legs, exoskeleton, 3 body segments |
| Arachnids | Spiders, scorpions | 8 legs, no antennae |
| Crustaceans | Crabs, lobsters, shrimp | Aquatic exoskeleton, gills |
| Mollusks | Octopus, clams, snails | Soft body, often with shell |
| Echinoderms | Starfish, sea urchins | 5-fold symmetry, water vascular system |
| Cnidarians | Jellyfish, coral, anemones | Stinging cells (nematocysts) |

**By numbers:**
- ~8.7 million total animal species estimated
- Only ~2 million formally described
- Insects represent ~80% of all known animal species
generalKnowledge.what is the rarest animal:
### World's Rarest Animals

**Critically Endangered species (selected):**

1. **Amur Leopard** (*Panthera pardus orientalis*) — ~100 remain in Russian Far East/NE China
2. **Javan Rhino** (*Rhinoceros sondaicus*) — ~76 in Ujung Kulon National Park, Indonesia only
3. **Vaquita** (*Phocoena sinus*) — ~8–10 remaining; world's most endangered marine mammal; Gulf of California
4. **Northern White Rhino** (*Ceratotherium simum cottoni*) — 2 remain (both female); functionally extinct
5. **Sumatran Orangutan** (*Pongo abelii*) — ~13,000 remain; deforestation threat
6. **Spix's Macaw** (*Cyanopsitta spixii*) — Extinct in wild since 2000; ~160 in captivity; reintroduction in Brazil 2022
7. **Saola** (*Pseudoryx nghetinhensis*) — 'Asian unicorn'; possibly <100 remain in Vietnam/Laos; last photographed in 2013

**Key drivers of extinction:**
- Habitat loss and deforestation
- Poaching and illegal wildlife trade
- Climate change
- Invasive species
- Pollution

The current extinction rate is estimated to be **100–1,000× higher** than the natural background rate — many scientists call this the **Sixth Mass Extinction**.
generalKnowledge.what is migration:
### Animal Migration

**Migration** is the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another, driven by food availability, breeding, or climate.

**Most extreme migrations:**

**Arctic Tern (*Sterna paradisaea*):**
- Migrates from Arctic to Antarctic and back — **70,000–90,000 km round trip** (longest migration of any animal)
- Sees more daylight than any other creature on Earth

**Monarch Butterfly (*Danaus plexippus*):**
- Travels up to **4,500 km** from eastern North America to central Mexico
- Individual butterflies make the complete southward journey — but it takes 3–5 generations to return north
- Navigate using a sun compass calibrated by circadian clock

**Wildebeest (Great Migration, Africa):**
- ~1.5 million wildebeest + 500,000 zebras and gazelles circle the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem (~3,000 km annually)
- Cross crocodile-filled Mara River twice per year in massive, dramatic herds

**Gray Whale:**
- Round trip of ~20,000 km — North Pacific feeding grounds to Mexican breeding lagoons and back

**Leatherback Sea Turtle:**
- Travels up to 20,000 km from nesting beaches in Indonesia to foraging grounds off the US East Coast

**Navigation methods used by animals:**
- Magnetic field sensing (birds, sea turtles, salmon)
- Star maps (birds, dung beetles)
- Polarized light (insects)
- Chemical gradients / olfaction (salmon returning to birth streams)
- Infrasound landmarks
generalKnowledge.tell me about crocodiles:
### Saltwater Crocodile (*Crocodylus porosus*)

Crocodiles are the **world's largest reptiles** and living descendants of archosaurs — their lineage stretches back over 200 million years.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** Saltwater croc up to 1,000 kg; length up to 6–7 m
- **Speed:** Up to 17 km/h on land; 24–29 km/h in water for short bursts
- **Lifespan:** 70–100 years in the wild
- **Bite force:** ~16,000 N — the **strongest bite of any animal ever measured**
- **Habitat:** Saltwater and brackish coastal habitats, rivers, estuaries across Southeast Asia and northern Australia

**Biology:**
- **Ectothermic** (cold-blooded) — rely on environment to regulate body temperature
- **Cannot chew** — tear prey with death rolls and swallow chunks whole
- **Stomach stones (gastroliths)** help grind food and regulate buoyancy
- **4-chambered heart** — most advanced of all reptiles; nearly identical to birds and mammals
- Can hold breath for up to **2 hours** when at rest

**Hunting:**
- Ambush predators — wait motionless for hours near the water's edge
- 'Death roll': grab prey and spin violently to tear off chunks
- Prey: fish, birds, mammals including deer, buffalo, even sharks

**Conservation:**
- Saltwater crocodile: **Least Concern** — recovered from near-extinction thanks to 1970s protections
- Nile crocodile (~4,000–5,000 animals per year kill more humans than any other large predator)
generalKnowledge.tell me about hippos:
### Hippopotamus (*Hippopotamus amphibius*)

The hippopotamus is the **third-largest land animal** and one of the most dangerous animals in Africa — responsible for an estimated 500+ human deaths per year.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 1,500–3,000 kg (males); females 1,300–2,000 kg
- **Length:** Up to 5 m; shoulder height ~1.5 m
- **Speed:** Up to 30 km/h on land — faster than a human
- **Lifespan:** 40–50 years in the wild
- **Habitat:** Sub-Saharan Africa, rivers, lakes, and wetlands

**Biology:**
- Closest living relatives: **whales and dolphins** (diverged ~55 million years ago)
- Spend up to **16 hours per day** submerged to stay cool
- Cannot swim — walk and bounce along the river bottom
- **Blood sweat:** Secrete a reddish, oily fluid (not actual blood) that acts as sunscreen, moisturizer, and antibiotic
- Eyes, ears, and nostrils positioned on top of the skull — can hear, see, and breathe while almost entirely submerged

**Diet:**
- Herbivorous — graze on grass at night (up to 40 kg per night); travel up to 10 km from water
- Their dung fertilizes rivers, supporting fish populations

**Social behavior:**
- Live in groups ('bloats') of 10–30; dominant bull controls territory
- Extremely territorial in water; highly aggressive

**Conservation:**
- **Vulnerable** — ~115,000–130,000 remain; declining due to habitat loss and hunting
generalKnowledge.tell me about giraffes:
### Giraffe (*Giraffa camelopardalis*)

The giraffe is the **tallest living terrestrial animal on Earth** — an icon of the African savanna.

**Key facts:**
- **Height:** Up to 5.8 m (males); females up to 4.6 m
- **Weight:** Males 800–1,930 kg; females 550–1,200 kg
- **Speed:** Up to 60 km/h; sustained 50 km/h over longer distances
- **Lifespan:** 25 years in the wild; up to 40 in captivity
- **Habitat:** African savannas, grasslands, open woodlands

**Biology:**
- **Neck:** Up to 1.8 m long — contains only 7 cervical vertebrae (same as humans), each elongated
- **Heart:** Weighs ~11 kg (largest of any land mammal); generates 2× normal blood pressure to pump blood up the long neck
- **Blood pressure control:** Specialized valves and thick-walled vessels prevent blood rushing to the head when bending to drink
- **Tongue:** ~45–50 cm long, dark purple-blue (melanin-rich, protecting against sunburn)
- Newborns fall ~1.8 m at birth and stand within an hour

**Diet:**
- Browse on acacia, mimosa, and combretum trees — up to 34 kg of leaves per day
- Acacia thorns don't deter them; thick saliva coats any swallowed thorns

**Social structure:**
- Semi-social; loose herds; males fight with 'necking' (slamming necks together)

**Conservation:**
- **Vulnerable** — ~117,000 remain (declined 40% in 30 years); 4 recognized species; poaching and habitat loss are main threats
generalKnowledge.tell me about rhinos:
### Rhinoceros

Rhinoceroses are massive **odd-toed ungulates** (Perissodactyla) and some of the largest land animals alive — and among the most critically endangered.

**5 species:**
- **White Rhino** — largest; ~2,300 kg; two subspecies (southern: ~15,000; northern: 2 females remain — functionally extinct)
- **Black Rhino** — ~800–1,400 kg; Critically Endangered (~5,600 remain)
- **Indian (Greater One-Horned) Rhino** — ~1,800–2,700 kg; Vulnerable (~3,700)
- **Sumatran Rhino** — smallest (~700 kg); Critically Endangered (~34 survive)
- **Javan Rhino** — rarest large mammal on Earth; ~76 survive in one Indonesian park

**Key facts:**
- **Horn:** Made of keratin (same as human hair and nails), not bone; can reach 1.5 m; grows ~3 cm/year
- **Skin:** 1.5–5 cm thick; looks armored but is sensitive to sunburn and insects → mud wallowing provides SPF
- **Speed:** Up to 55 km/h (black rhino) — despite their size
- **Lifespan:** 40–50 years
- **Diet:** Herbivores — white rhinos graze grass; black rhinos browse shrubs and trees

**Conservation crisis:**
- Poaching for horn (used in traditional Asian medicine; sold for up to $65,000/kg — more valuable than gold)
- All five species protected under CITES Appendix I
- Dehorning programs and intensive anti-poaching patrols protect key populations
generalKnowledge.tell me about zebras:
### Zebra

Zebras are **wild equids** native to Africa, instantly recognizable by their bold black-and-white stripe patterns — every zebra's pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.

**3 species:**
- **Plains Zebra** (*Equus quagga*) — most common; ~500,000; East and Southern Africa
- **Mountain Zebra** — Vulnerable; ~35,000 remain
- **Grévy's Zebra** — largest; Endangered; ~2,800 remain

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 200–450 kg
- **Speed:** Up to 65 km/h; sustained 56 km/h
- **Lifespan:** 20–30 years in the wild
- **Height:** ~1.2–1.5 m at shoulder

**Stripes — why?**
- Current best evidence: **deter biting flies** — insects have difficulty landing on moving striped patterns
- Also: heat regulation (stripes may create micro air currents), individual recognition, social bonding
- Stripes are only in the coat — the skin beneath is uniformly dark

**Social structure:**
- Plains zebras form **harems** — one dominant stallion with multiple mares and foals
- Groups join together in massive herds during the Great Migration (with wildebeest and gazelles)
- Groom each other for social bonding; mutual alertness helps detect predators

**Predators:**
- Lions, leopards, hyenas, crocodiles (during river crossings)
- Defend themselves with powerful kicks — can kill a lion

**Conservation:**
- Plains zebra: Least Concern; Grévy's: Endangered; threats include habitat loss and hunting
generalKnowledge.tell me about koalas:
### Koala (*Phascolarctos cinereus*)

The koala is an **arboreal marsupial** native to Australia — not a bear, but closer to wombats on the evolutionary tree.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 4–15 kg (males larger; vary by region)
- **Body length:** 60–85 cm
- **Lifespan:** 13–18 years in the wild
- **Sleep:** Up to **18–22 hours per day** — one of the sleepiest mammals
- **Habitat:** Eastern and southeastern Australia; eucalyptus forests

**Diet:**
- Almost exclusively **eucalyptus leaves** — toxic to most animals
- Specialized liver detoxifies the compounds; gut bacteria help digest the tough cellulose
- Eucalyptus is low in nutrition and calories — hence the extreme sleeping to conserve energy
- Adults eat 200–500 g of leaves per day from only ~50 of the 700+ eucalyptus species

**Marsupial biology:**
- Joeys born tiny (~2 cm, ~0.5 g) after just 35 days gestation
- Crawl to the mother's backward-facing pouch (unusual for marsupials); stay 6–7 months
- Mothers feed joeys 'pap' — a specialized, bacteria-rich form of feces that seeds the joey's gut with the microbes needed to digest eucalyptus

**Unique features:**
- Fingerprints nearly identical to human fingerprints (convergent evolution)
- Koalas rarely need to drink — the word 'koala' may derive from an Aboriginal word meaning 'no water'

**Conservation:**
- Listed as **Endangered** in Australia (2022) — population ~100,000; threats: habitat loss, chlamydia disease (affects up to 50%), wildfires, vehicle strikes
generalKnowledge.tell me about kangaroos:
### Kangaroo

Kangaroos are the **largest marsupials** in the world and the iconic symbol of Australia — the only large animals to use **hopping as their primary means of locomotion**.

**4 species of 'true' kangaroos:**
- **Red Kangaroo** — largest; males up to 90 kg, 1.8 m tall
- **Eastern Grey Kangaroo** — most numerous
- **Western Grey Kangaroo**
- **Antilopine Kangaroo** — tropical north Australia

**Key facts:**
- **Speed:** Up to **71 km/h** (red kangaroo); sustained 40 km/h
- **Jumping:** 9 m in a single bound; up to 3 m high
- **Lifespan:** 23 years in the wild
- **Hopping efficiency:** Tendons in hind legs store and release elastic energy — hopping is more efficient than running at high speeds (energy cost stays constant above ~15 km/h)

**Marsupial biology:**
- Joey born after ~33 days gestation — size of a grape (~1 g)
- Climbs unaided to the pouch; stays ~8 months, then 'at foot' until ~18 months
- Females can have **3 simultaneous offspring** at different developmental stages
- **Embryonic diapause** — can pause a developing embryo's growth if resources are scarce

**Social structure:**
- Groups ('mobs') of 10–100; dominant male ('boomer') defends females
- Males box to establish dominance — using forelimbs and sharp hind claws

**Conservation:**
- All four species: **Least Concern** — combined population ~50 million
- Kangaroos are more numerous than Australia's human population
generalKnowledge.tell me about pandas:
### Giant Panda (*Ailuropoda melanoleuca*)

The giant panda is one of the world's most recognized and beloved animals — a symbol of wildlife conservation globally.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 70–120 kg
- **Length:** 1.2–1.8 m; shoulder height ~70–80 cm
- **Lifespan:** 14–20 years in the wild; up to 30 in captivity
- **Habitat:** Mountainous bamboo forests of south-central China (Sichuan, Shaanxi, Gansu provinces)
- **Wild population:** ~1,864 (2021 census) — upgraded from Endangered to **Vulnerable** in 2021

**Diet:**
- 99% **bamboo** — up to 12–38 kg per day, 12–16 hours of eating
- Technically carnivores by ancestry (bears) with a herbivore diet; digestive system still short like a carnivore's — hence must eat enormous quantities
- Have a **pseudo-thumb** — an enlarged radial sesamoid bone that works like an opposable thumb for gripping bamboo
- Also eat small rodents, fish, and insects occasionally

**Reproduction:**
- Among the most difficult breeders in captivity — females fertile only 1–3 days per year
- Cubs born extremely small (~85–140 g — 1/900th of mother's weight) and are entirely helpless
- Conservation breeding programs at Chengdu and Wolong centers have helped stabilize the population

**Black and white coloring:** Still not fully explained — possible camouflage, temperature regulation (white reflects cold), or social signaling
generalKnowledge.tell me about snow leopards:
### Snow Leopard (*Panthera uncia*)

The snow leopard is the **apex predator of the high mountains** of Central Asia — a ghost-like, elusive cat rarely seen in the wild.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 22–55 kg (relatively light for a big cat)
- **Length:** 1–1.3 m body; tail 80–100 cm (longest tail relative to body of any cat — used for balance and as a blanket)
- **Speed:** Up to 64 km/h; can leap 9 m horizontally and 3 m vertically
- **Lifespan:** 10–12 years wild; up to 21 in captivity
- **Habitat:** Rocky, mountainous terrain at 3,000–5,500 m altitude across 12 countries (including China, India, Nepal, Mongolia)
- **Wild population:** ~4,000–6,500 — **Vulnerable** on IUCN Red List

**High-altitude adaptations:**
- **Large nasal passages** warm cold air before it reaches the lungs
- **Wide, fur-covered paws** act as snowshoes
- **Thick fur** (up to 12 cm on the belly) insulates against −40°C
- **Low-oxygen adaptation:** High lung capacity for thin-air breathing

**Hunting:**
- Prey: blue sheep (bharal), ibex, argali sheep, marmots, domestic livestock
- Stalk prey, then leap from above — can kill prey 3× their own weight
- Cannot roar (lacks fully ossified hyoid bone) — instead 'chuff,' hiss, and mew

**Threats:**
- Poaching for fur and bones, retaliatory killing by herders, climate change shrinking habitat, prey depletion
generalKnowledge.tell me about jaguars:
### Jaguar (*Panthera onca*)

The jaguar is the **largest cat in the Americas** and the third-largest in the world — a powerful, adaptable apex predator.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** 57–113 kg (males); females 36–80 kg
- **Length:** 1.2–1.9 m body + 45–75 cm tail
- **Speed:** Up to 80 km/h in short bursts
- **Lifespan:** 12–15 years wild; up to 23 in captivity
- **Habitat:** Amazon basin, Pantanal, Central America; historically from SW USA to Patagonia
- **IUCN Status:** **Near Threatened** — ~64,000 remain (range reduced by ~50%)

**Distinctive features:**
- Rosette markings (like leopards) but jaguars have spots inside the rosettes — distinguishes them from leopards
- **Melanistic (black) jaguars** exist — the 'black panther' — rosettes still visible in sunlight

**Bite force:**
- Strongest bite force relative to size of any big cat: can crush turtle shells and caiman skulls
- Unique killing method: pierces the skull directly between the ears rather than biting the throat

**Diet & behavior:**
- Apex predator; eats ~85 species including caiman, capybara, deer, fish, giant river otters
- Excellent swimmers — actively hunts in rivers (unusual for cats)
- Solitary and territorial; males hold 25–150 km² ranges

**Cultural significance:**
- Sacred to Aztec, Maya, and Inca civilizations — symbol of power, night, and the underworld

**Threats:**
- Deforestation (particularly in the Amazon), ranching conflicts, illegal wildlife trade
generalKnowledge.tell me about orcas:
### Orca / Killer Whale (*Orcinus orca*)

The orca is the **largest member of the dolphin family** and one of the most powerful and intelligent apex predators on Earth.

**Key facts:**
- **Weight:** Males up to 6,000 kg; females up to 3,500 kg
- **Length:** Males up to 8–9 m; females 5–7 m
- **Speed:** Up to 56 km/h — one of the fastest marine mammals
- **Lifespan:** Males 30–40 years; females up to 80–90 years (post-reproductive females can live decades past menopause)
- **Habitat:** Every ocean — from Arctic to Antarctic; no natural predators

**Intelligence & culture:**
- Among the **most socially complex animals** — matrilineal family pods are the core unit
- Different **ecotypes** (resident, transient, offshore) have distinct diets, vocalizations, and behaviors — essentially different cultures
- **Vocal dialects:** Each pod has unique calls; calves learn their pod's dialect
- **Cooperative hunting:** Coordinate like wolves; wave-wash seals off ice floes; corral fish into 'bait balls'; teach hunting techniques to offspring

**Diet varies by ecotype:**
- Resident orcas: primarily fish (Chinook salmon)
- Transient orcas: marine mammals (seals, dolphins, even blue whales)
- Offshore orcas: sharks and rays

**Remarkable behavior:**
- Spy-hop (rise vertically to survey surroundings)
- Beach themselves momentarily to grab seal pups
- Use kelp beds as tools to scrub parasites

**Conservation:**
- No single global status; some populations critically endangered (Southern Resident orcas: ~73 left)
- Threats: prey depletion, ocean noise, pollution (PCBs accumulate up the food chain)
generalKnowledge.tell me about blue whales:
### Blue Whale (*Balaenoptera musculus*)

The blue whale is the **largest animal ever known to have existed on Earth** — dwarfing even the largest dinosaurs.

**Key facts:**
- **Length:** Up to 33 m (108 ft)
- **Weight:** Up to 180 metric tons (200 short tons)
- **Heart:** Size of a small car (~180 kg); pumps ~220 L of blood per beat
- **Speed:** Cruises at 20 km/h; can reach 48 km/h when alarmed
- **Lifespan:** 80–110 years
- **Habitat:** All oceans; migrate between polar feeding and tropical breeding grounds

**Feeding:**
- Filter feeder — eats almost exclusively **krill** (tiny shrimp-like crustaceans)
- Consumes up to **40 million krill per day** (~3,600 kg)
- Lunge feeding: accelerates to high speed then opens mouth, engulfing huge water volume; baleen plates (keratin) filter krill
- Tongue alone weighs ~2,700 kg

**Calls:**
- Blue whale calls reach **188 decibels** — among the loudest sounds produced by any animal
- Low-frequency moans (10–40 Hz) travel **hundreds to thousands of km** through ocean
- Used for communication and likely mate finding

**Conservation:**
- **Endangered** — commercial whaling reduced population from ~350,000 to as few as 5,000–8,000 by mid-20th century
- Protected globally since 1966; current estimate: 10,000–25,000
- Threats: ship strikes, entanglement in fishing gear, climate change reducing krill populations
- Recovery extremely slow due to low reproduction rate (one calf every 2–3 years)
generalKnowledge.tell me about manta rays:
### Manta Ray (*Mobula birostris / Mobula alfredi*)

Manta rays are the **largest rays in the world** — gentle, filter-feeding giants that glide through tropical and subtropical oceans.

**Key facts:**
- **Wingspan:** Giant manta ray up to 7 m (23 ft)
- **Weight:** Up to 1,350 kg
- **Speed:** Up to 24 km/h; capable of leaping clear of the water
- **Lifespan:** Up to 40 years
- **Habitat:** Tropical and subtropical open ocean and coastal habitats; worldwide distribution
- **IUCN Status:** Giant oceanic manta — **Endangered**; reef manta — **Vulnerable**

**Feeding:**
- Filter feed on plankton and small fish using specialized gill plates (not gill rakers)
- Cephalic fins (horn-like projections on head) funnel water into the mouth
- Must keep swimming to maintain water flow over gills
- Feed near the surface, often at 'cleaning stations' where fish remove parasites

**Intelligence:**
- Largest brain of any fish, relative to body size
- One of the few non-mammalian animals to pass the **mirror self-recognition test**
- Observed to swim in loops around sources of artificial light — possible play behavior

**Biology:**
- Unlike stingrays, manta rays have **no venomous tail spine**
- Give birth to live young; 1 pup every 2 years
- Skeleton: entirely cartilage

**Threats:**
- Targeted for gill plates used in traditional Chinese medicine; bycatch; boat strikes; ocean plastic ingestion
generalKnowledge.tell me about hammerhead sharks:
### Hammerhead Shark (*Sphyrna* spp.)

Hammerhead sharks are among the most distinctive sharks, recognized by their unique **cephalofoil** — the wide, flattened, hammer-shaped head.

**9 species, key ones:**
- **Great Hammerhead** — largest; up to 6 m, 580 kg; Critically Endangered
- **Scalloped Hammerhead** — forms enormous schools; Critically Endangered
- **Smooth Hammerhead** — Vulnerable
- **Bonnethead** — smallest; ~1 m; omnivorous (eats seagrass)

**Why the hammer-head?**
- **360° binocular vision** — eyes at the extreme ends of the cephalofoil give overlapping forward and backward vision
- **Amplified electroreception** — sensory pores (ampullae of Lorenzini) spread across the wide head detect the bioelectric fields of buried prey (stingrays) with extraordinary precision — essentially a metal detector
- **Enhanced maneuverability** — acts as a hydrodynamic wing for agile turning

**Key facts:**
- **Diet:** Stingrays (primary), bony fish, squid, crustaceans, other sharks
- **Speed:** Up to 25 km/h
- **Lifespan:** 20–30 years
- Often found with stingray barbs embedded in their mouths — apparently immune to the venom

**Behavior:**
- Scalloped hammerheads school in hundreds during the day; split to hunt alone at night
- Schools at seamounts may be navigation landmarks or social aggregations

**Conservation:**
- Heavily targeted for fins (shark fin soup); all species declining; Great and Scalloped: **Critically Endangered**
generalKnowledge.tell me about bald eagles:
### Bald Eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*)

The bald eagle is the **national symbol of the United States** and one of North America's most spectacular birds of prey.

**Key facts:**
- **Wingspan:** 1.8–2.4 m (females larger than males)
- **Weight:** 3–6.3 kg
- **Speed:** ~56–70 km/h in level flight; dives at up to 160 km/h
- **Lifespan:** 20–30 years in the wild
- **Habitat:** Near large open water with abundant food and old-growth trees for nesting; across North America

**Vision:**
- Can spot a fish from 1.5 km away
- 4–8× sharper than human vision; perceives UV light and polarized light
- Two foveas (areas of maximum visual acuity) per eye

**Feeding:**
- Opportunistic; primarily **fish** — caught with powerful talons in spectacular plunge-dives
- Also steals prey from other birds (kleptoparasitism) — Ben Franklin famously objected to its selection as a national symbol for this reason
- Also eats waterfowl, rabbits, carrion

**Nests:**
- Build the **largest nests of any North American bird** — some over 3 m across, 1 m deep, weighing up to 1,000 kg
- Return to the same nest year after year, adding material each season

**Conservation success story:**
- Listed as Endangered in 1967 — only ~417 nesting pairs remained in the lower 48 states (DDT thinned eggshells)
- DDT banned 1972; protected under Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act
- Removed from endangered list **2007** — now ~316,000 individuals in the lower 48 states

**Lifespan mates:** Typically mate for life; re-mate only if partner dies
generalKnowledge.tell me about owls:
### Owls (Order Strigiformes)

Owls are **nocturnal birds of prey** — specialized aerial hunters with extraordinary senses adapted for hunting in darkness.

**~250 species worldwide**, from the tiny Elf Owl (31 g) to the Blakiston's Fish Owl (4.6 kg).

**Adaptations for night hunting:**

**Eyes:**
- Enormous, forward-facing eyes — up to 3 cm in diameter (cannot move in the socket)
- **Tubular shape** (not spherical like most eyes) allows more light-gathering surface
- Rod-dominated retina — extremely sensitive in low light but mostly colorblind
- Vision is ~10× more sensitive than human vision in darkness
- Cannot swivel eyes → have evolved **270° neck rotation** (not 360°)

**Hearing:**
- Facial disc (the flat face) acts as a **parabolic dish** to funnel sound
- Many owls have **asymmetrically placed ears** — one higher than the other, allowing 3D sound triangulation
- Great Grey Owl can detect a mouse under 60 cm of snow by sound alone

**Silent flight:**
- Comb-like serrations on leading flight feathers break up turbulence
- Velvet-like surface on feathers absorbs sound
- Soft downy fringe silences air flowing over trailing edge

**Pellets:**
- Cannot digest bones, fur, or feathers → compact into oval pellets and regurgitate
- Pellet dissection reveals the prey eaten

**Species highlights:**
- **Barn Owl** — most widely distributed land bird on Earth; present on every continent except Antarctica
- **Great Horned Owl** — apex avian predator; kills skunks, hawks, other owls
- **Snowy Owl** — Arctic specialist; one of the heaviest owls; active by day in Arctic summer
generalKnowledge.tell me about cobras:
### Cobra (*Naja* and related genera)

Cobras are highly venomous snakes in the family Elapidae, famous for their intimidating **hood display** and potent neurotoxic venom.

**Key species:**
- **Indian (Spectacled) Cobra** (*Naja naja*) — widespread across South Asia; responsible for ~15,000 deaths/year in India alone
- **King Cobra** (*Ophiophagus hannah*) — longest venomous snake on Earth (up to 5.85 m)
- **Spitting Cobra** — can spit venom up to 2.5 m with remarkable accuracy targeting the eyes
- **Egyptian Cobra** (*Naja haje*) — historically used in Cleopatra's death legend

**Hood:**
- Formed by elongated ribs behind the head spreading the loose neck skin
- Used as a **threat display** — to appear larger to predators
- The 'spectacle' pattern on the Indian cobra's hood mimics large eyes

**Venom:**
- Primarily **neurotoxic** — blocks neuromuscular junctions, causing respiratory failure
- Also contains cytotoxins causing tissue destruction
- King cobra venom can kill an elephant in a few hours; kill a human in 15–30 minutes untreated
- Despite potent venom, cobras are responsible for much human death globally due to range overlap with densely populated South and Southeast Asia

**Key facts:**
- **Lifespan:** 20–25 years
- **Speed:** Up to 19 km/h
- **Diet:** Primarily other snakes (king cobra); rodents, frogs, birds (other cobras)
- King cobras are the only snakes known to build nests for their eggs

**Conservation:**
- Indian cobra: CITES Appendix II; protected in India; population pressures from habitat loss and killing
generalKnowledge.tell me about pythons:
### Python (*Pythonidae* family)

Pythons are among the **world's largest snakes** — non-venomous constrictors that kill prey by suffocation rather than venom.

**Key species:**
- **Reticulated Python** (*Malayopython reticulatus*) — **longest snake on Earth**; verified up to 7.67 m; can exceed 100 kg
- **Burmese Python** (*Python bivittatus*) — up to 5.5 m, 90 kg; Vulnerable; invasive in Florida Everglades
- **Ball Python** (*Python regius*) — small (1.2–1.8 m); most common pet snake; rolls into a ball when threatened
- **African Rock Python** (*Python sebae*) — up to 5.5 m; Africa's largest snake

**Constriction:**
- Grab prey with backward-curved teeth (to prevent escape), then coil around it
- Each exhale from the prey is met with tighter coils — suffocates rather than crushes
- Can detect when heart stops (ceases constriction at cardiac arrest)

**Key biology:**
- **Jacobson's organ:** Fork-tongue flicks collect scent particles for chemoreception
- **Heat pits:** Labial heat-sensing pits detect infrared radiation (body heat) of warm-blooded prey in total darkness — resolution of ~0.003°C
- **Flexible jaws:** Ligaments (not hinged) allow swallowing prey far larger than the head
- After a large meal, stomach acid pH drops to ~1; digestive enzymes double; intestines grow in size — metabolism can increase 40×

**Diet:**
- Rodents, pigs, deer, primates; large reticulated pythons can take sun bears and even small humans (rare cases documented)

**Conservation:**
- Reticulated python: least concern; Burmese python: Vulnerable; Ball python: near threatened; major trade pressures
generalKnowledge.tell me about anacondas:
### Anaconda (*Eunectes* spp.)

Anaconidas are the **heaviest snakes in the world** — semi-aquatic giants from South American river systems.

**Species:**
- **Green Anaconda** (*Eunectes murinus*) — **heaviest snake on Earth**; females up to 8.8 m, 227 kg; males significantly smaller (~3 m, 30 kg)
- **Yellow Anaconda** (*Eunectes notaeus*) — smaller; up to 4 m; southern South America
- **Northern Green Anaconda** (*Eunectes akayima*) — recently described as a distinct species (2024)

**Key facts:**
- **Habitat:** Amazon and Orinoco river basins; tropical rainforests and wetlands
- **Weight record:** 97.5 kg (verified); unverified claims up to 227 kg
- Females are substantially larger than males (one of the most pronounced sexual size dimorphisms in vertebrates)

**Aquatic life:**
- Spend most time in water — supported by buoyancy, which allows their massive weight
- Excellent swimmers; eyes and nostrils on top of head for surface breathing while nearly submerged
- Ambush prey at water's edge

**Diet & hunting:**
- Constrictor — suffocates prey then swallows whole
- Prey: fish, turtles, caimans, capybaras, deer, and occasionally jaguars
- Can go months to a year between large meals

**Reproduction:**
- **Viviparous** — give birth to live young (20–40 offspring); no eggs
- Breeding balls: multiple males coil around a single female for weeks

**Conservation:**
- No formal IUCN status; significant pressure from habitat loss and hunting
generalKnowledge.tell me about t-rex:
### Tyrannosaurus rex (*T. rex*)

T. rex was one of the **largest terrestrial predators ever to walk the Earth** — a theropod dinosaur that lived during the **Late Cretaceous** (~68–66 million years ago).

**Key facts (from fossil evidence):**
- **Length:** Up to 12–13 m
- **Height:** ~3.7 m at the hips
- **Weight:** Estimated 8,000–14,000 kg
- **Bite force:** ~35,000–57,000 N — the strongest bite force of any land animal ever (more powerful than any living animal)
- **Teeth:** Up to 30 cm long (banana-sized); serrated, bone-crushing; continuously replaced
- **Range:** Western North America (Hell Creek Formation — present-day Montana, Wyoming, the Dakotas)

**Speed:**
- Historically depicted as very fast (Jurassic Park); modern biomechanical models suggest ~12–25 km/h
- Large adults may have been limited to ~17 km/h without damaging leg bones

**Senses:**
- **Olfactory bulbs** disproportionately large — exceptional sense of smell
- **Forward-facing eyes** — binocular vision superior to modern hawks, useful for depth perception
- Hearing likely tuned to low frequencies

**Modern understanding:**
- Almost certainly had **feathers** at least during juvenile stages (smaller relatives clearly did)
- **Warm-blooded** (endothermic) — evidence from bone histology showing fast growth rates
- Forelimbs tiny but not vestigial — recent analysis suggests used for grasping during mating
- **Birds are living theropod dinosaurs** — T. rex's closest living relatives are chickens and ostriches

**Extinction:** Killed 66 million years ago by the Chicxulub asteroid impact (and subsequent volcanic winter), which wiped out ~75% of all species
generalKnowledge.tell me about velociraptors:
### Velociraptor (*Velociraptor mongoliensis*)

Velociraptor was a **small, feathered theropod dinosaur** of the Late Cretaceous (~75–71 million years ago) — famous from *Jurassic Park* but very different from its Hollywood depiction.

**Real Velociraptor (vs. movie version):**
| Feature | Real Velociraptor | Jurassic Park 'Raptor' |
|---------|------------------|------------------------|
| Size | Turkey-sized; ~15 kg | Human-sized; ~60–80 kg |
| Feathers | Yes — quill knobs on arm bones prove it | No feathers |
| Snout | Long, flat, crocodilian | More rounded |
| Speed | ~25 km/h | Depicted faster |

*(The movie 'raptors' were actually based on Deinonychus or Utahraptor.)*

**Key biology:**
- **Length:** ~2 m; hip height ~50 cm
- **Sickle claw:** Large curved claw on the second toe — used to pin and slash prey, not disembowel (new research suggests it held prey down while the jaws did the killing)
- **Intelligence:** Among the smarter non-avian dinosaurs; relatively large brain-to-body ratio
- **Warm-blooded** — rapid growth rates in bone evidence

**Habitat:**
- Desert/semi-arid environment of what is now Mongolia and northern China
- Famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil: a Velociraptor and Protoceratops locked in combat, preserved by a collapsing sand dune

**Evolutionary context:**
- Closely related to modern birds; belongs to the deinonychosauria clade
- Its feathered arms were too short for flight — likely used for brooding eggs or display
generalKnowledge.tell me about mammoths:
### Woolly Mammoth (*Mammuthus primigenius*)

The woolly mammoth was an **Ice Age giant** — a relative of modern elephants that thrived in the cold grasslands of the northern hemisphere.

**Key facts:**
- **Existed:** ~400,000 years ago to ~4,000 years ago (small island population on Wrangel Island survived until ~2000 BC)
- **Size:** Similar to African elephants — 2.7–3.4 m tall; ~6,000 kg
- **Tusks:** Up to 3.5–4 m long; curved; used to sweep snow from vegetation and fight
- **Lifespan:** ~60–80 years (based on dental evidence)
- **Habitat:** Mammoth steppe — grasslands stretching from Spain to Alaska and Siberia; adapted to cold climates

**Cold adaptations:**
- **Thick, layered coat:** 8–10 cm underfur plus 90 cm outer guard hairs
- **Fat layer:** Up to 10 cm thick for insulation
- **Small ears:** Reduced surface area to minimize heat loss (cf. African elephant's large heat-dissipating ears)
- **Specialized hemoglobin:** Delivered oxygen to muscles efficiently at low temperatures
- **Trunk adaptation:** Could dig through snow to find vegetation

**Diet:**
- Grazed on grasses, sedges, shrubs, and herbs — 180 kg of vegetation per day

**Extinction debate:**
- Died out ~10,000 years ago (mainland); causes debated: climate warming (grassland habitat shrank) + **human hunting pressure** (humans arrived in their range and targeted them for meat, fat, ivory, and bone for shelters)
- Most likely: combination of both factors

**De-extinction:**
- Colossal Biosciences and Revive & Restore working to create a mammoth-elephant hybrid by 2028 using CRISPR gene editing of Asian elephant DNA
generalKnowledge.how fast is a cheetah:
### Cheetah Speed

The cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is the **fastest land animal on Earth**.

- **Top speed:** 112–120 km/h (70–75 mph) over 200–300 m
- **Acceleration:** 0 to 96 km/h in approximately 3 seconds
- **Stride:** Up to 7–8 meters at full speed; feet leave the ground ~50% of the time

After a chase, cheetahs must rest 15–30 minutes to cool down before eating. Their prey is often stolen by lions and hyenas during this recovery.

For full cheetah facts → ask **'tell me about cheetahs'**
generalKnowledge.what do lions eat:
### Lion Diet

Lions are **obligate carnivores** and apex predators. Their diet includes:

- **Primary prey:** zebra, wildebeest, buffalo, warthog, giraffe, impala
- **Opportunistic:** small mammals, birds, reptiles, and carrion
- **Amount:** ~7 kg of meat per day on average; can eat 30+ kg in a single sitting

Female lions do approximately **90% of the hunting**, typically at night using coordinated ambush tactics. Males defend the pride's territory and cubs.

For full lion facts → ask **'tell me about lions'**
generalKnowledge.where do penguins live:
### Where Penguins Live

Penguins live **exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere**:

- Most species: **Antarctica, sub-Antarctic islands, southern coasts of South America, South Africa, and New Zealand**
- **Galápagos Penguin** — only species living near the equator (Galápagos Islands)
- **African Penguin** — coast of South Africa and Namibia
- **Little Blue Penguin** — southern Australia and New Zealand

All 18 species depend on cold, nutrient-rich waters for their fish and squid diet. None naturally live in the Arctic.

For full penguin facts → ask **'tell me about penguins'**
generalKnowledge.facts about dolphins:
### Dolphin Facts

- **Most intelligent marine animals** — self-aware, use tools, have signature whistles (unique names)
- **Echolocation:** Emit clicks up to 200,000 Hz to map their environment in 3D; fine enough to detect a golf ball at 75 m
- **Speed:** Bottlenose dolphin ~37 km/h; common dolphin up to 60 km/h
- **Lifespan:** 20–50 years depending on species
- **Social:** Live in fluid 'fission-fusion' societies; form long-term alliances
- **~90 species** including orcas, porpoises, and river dolphins
- **Diet:** Fish, squid, crustaceans
- **Threats:** Bycatch, ocean noise pollution, hunting

For full dolphin facts → ask **'tell me about dolphins'**
generalKnowledge.how fast is a lion:
### Lion Speed

Lions can reach speeds of up to **80 km/h (50 mph)** in short bursts of 90–100 m.

- They typically stalk prey to within 30 m before charging
- Lions tire quickly and rely on coordinated group tactics
- Females are typically slightly faster than males due to their smaller size
- Average sustained pursuit speed: ~55–60 km/h

For full lion facts → ask **'tell me about lions'**
generalKnowledge.how fast is a shark:
### Shark Speed

Speeds vary by species:

- **Shortfin Mako Shark** — fastest shark; up to **70 km/h**
- **Great White Shark** — ~56 km/h in short bursts; cruises at ~25 km/h
- **Whale Shark** — slow; ~5 km/h (filter feeder)
- **Hammerhead** — up to 25 km/h

For full shark facts → ask **'tell me about sharks'**
generalKnowledge.how big is a blue whale:
### Blue Whale Size

The blue whale is the **largest animal ever known to exist**:

- **Length:** Up to 33 m (108 ft)
- **Weight:** Up to 180 metric tons (200 short tons)
- **Heart:** Size of a small car (~180 kg)
- **Tongue:** Weighs ~2,700 kg alone
- **Newborn calf:** ~7 m long, ~2,700 kg — among the largest newborns of any animal

For full blue whale facts → ask **'tell me about blue whales'**
generalKnowledge.where do polar bears live:
### Where Polar Bears Live

Polar bears (*Ursus maritimus*) live in the **Arctic Circle** region:

- **Countries:** Canada (most bears), Russia, Norway (Svalbard), Greenland, and the United States (Alaska)
- **Habitat:** Sea ice over the Arctic Ocean, coastal areas, and islands
- **Range:** 5 subpopulations across the circumpolar Arctic
- They are classified as **marine mammals** because they depend almost entirely on the sea for food (primarily ringed seals)

Global warming is critically threatening their habitat — Arctic sea ice is declining ~13% per decade.

For full polar bear facts → ask **'tell me about polar bears'**
generalKnowledge.what do elephants eat:
### Elephant Diet

Elephants are **herbivores** with enormous appetites:

- **Daily intake:** 140–270 kg of vegetation per day
- **Food:** Grasses, leaves, bark, fruit, roots, and bamboo
- **Water:** Drink 150–300 liters per day; can smell water from 20 km away
- **Digestion:** Only ~40% efficient — large amounts of undigested plant matter passes through
- Elephants 'create' environments by knocking down trees, allowing grasslands to form
- Seed dispersers — swallow and spread fruit seeds over vast areas in their dung

For full elephant facts → ask **'tell me about elephants'**
generalKnowledge.what do tigers eat: Tigers are apex carnivores that prey primarily on large ungulates such as deer, wild boar, and gaur. A tiger can eat up to 40 kg of meat in a single meal and may go days between kills, hunting alone using stealth and a powerful ambush technique.
generalKnowledge.what do wolves eat: Wolves are highly adaptable carnivores whose diet centers on large hoofed mammals — elk, moose, bison, caribou, and deer. They hunt cooperatively in packs and will supplement their diet with smaller prey like rabbits, beavers, and even berries when large prey is scarce.
generalKnowledge.what do sharks eat: Shark diets vary by species: great whites target marine mammals like seals and sea lions, hammerheads favor stingrays and fish, and whale sharks filter-feed on plankton and small fish. Most sharks are opportunistic predators, using electroreception to detect prey.
generalKnowledge.what do dolphins eat: Dolphins are carnivores that eat primarily fish, squid, and crustaceans. They use echolocation to locate prey and often hunt cooperatively, herding fish into tight 'bait balls' before taking turns feeding.
generalKnowledge.what do eagles eat: Eagles are apex avian predators that eat fish, small mammals, birds, and carrion depending on the species. Bald eagles specialize in fish, while golden eagles hunt rabbits, ground squirrels, and prairie dogs. Their powerful talons kill prey on impact.
generalKnowledge.what do gorillas eat: Gorillas are primarily herbivores, feeding on leaves, stems, bark, fruit, and flowers — up to 18 kg of plant matter per day. Western lowland gorillas eat more fruit than mountain gorillas. They occasionally eat small insects and ants for protein.
generalKnowledge.what do cheetahs eat: Cheetahs are obligate carnivores that hunt gazelles, impalas, rabbits, and young wildebeest. Unlike most big cats, they hunt by day using explosive speed rather than stealth, killing prey with a throat bite that causes suffocation.
generalKnowledge.what do penguins eat: Penguins eat fish, squid, and krill, which they catch by diving underwater — some species can dive to 500 m. They swallow prey whole underwater and their backward-pointing tongue spines prevent fish from escaping.
generalKnowledge.what do polar bears eat: Polar bears are hypercarnivores that depend almost entirely on ringed and bearded seals for sustenance, ambushing them at breathing holes in the ice. In summer when sea ice retreats, they may eat berries, kelp, and bird eggs, but can lose hundreds of kilograms of body weight without seal fat.
generalKnowledge.what do bees eat: Bees feed on nectar (a sugar solution from flowers) and pollen (their protein source). Worker bees convert nectar into honey by evaporating water and adding enzymes; this stored honey feeds the hive through winter. Larvae are fed royal jelly, pollen, and honey.
generalKnowledge.what do crocodiles eat: Crocodiles are ambush predators that eat fish, birds, mammals, and carrion. Large saltwater and Nile crocodiles can take prey as large as buffalo or wildebeest by grabbing them at the water's edge and performing a 'death roll' to tear off pieces. They can go months without food.
generalKnowledge.what do hippos eat: Despite their fearsome reputation, hippos are primarily herbivores, grazing on grass at night — consuming up to 40 kg of grass per evening. They rarely eat meat, though they are known to scavenge or cannibalize in rare cases, likely driven by nutritional deficiencies.
generalKnowledge.what do giraffes eat: Giraffes are herbivores that feed mainly on acacia and mimosa leaves, flowers, and pods, consuming up to 34 kg per day. Their long prehensile tongue (45–50 cm) and thick lips allow them to strip leaves from thorny branches. They rarely need to drink due to moisture in their food.
generalKnowledge.what do rhinos eat: Rhinos are strict herbivores. White rhinos are grazers, eating grasses close to the ground, while black rhinos are browsers, using their pointed upper lip to grasp leaves, twigs, and shrubs. Both can consume 50–90 kg of plant material daily.
generalKnowledge.what do zebras eat: Zebras are grazers that feed almost exclusively on grasses, preferring tall coarse grasses that other animals avoid. They use their strong incisor teeth to clip grass close to the ground and can travel long distances to find fresh pasture and water.
generalKnowledge.what do koalas eat: Koalas are highly specialized herbivores that eat almost exclusively eucalyptus leaves — choosing about 50 out of 700+ species. The leaves are toxic and low in nutrition, so koalas sleep up to 22 hours a day to conserve energy and detoxify their food.
generalKnowledge.what do kangaroos eat: Kangaroos are herbivorous grazers and browsers that eat grasses, leaves, shrubs, and flowering plants. Red kangaroos eat mainly dry grasses while tree kangaroos prefer leaves and fruit. They have a chambered stomach similar to ruminants, allowing them to regurgitate and re-chew food.
generalKnowledge.what do pandas eat: Giant pandas subsist almost entirely on bamboo — eating 12–38 kg of bamboo shoots, stems, and leaves per day for up to 16 hours. Despite being classified as carnivores (family Ursidae), their gut bacteria and skull structure have adapted to this plant-heavy diet. They occasionally eat eggs, small birds, or rodents.
generalKnowledge.what do snow leopards eat: Snow leopards are carnivores that prey primarily on blue sheep (bharal) and ibex in their high-mountain habitat. They are capable of killing prey up to three times their own body weight and will cache large kills to feed on for several days.
generalKnowledge.what do jaguars eat: Jaguars are apex carnivores with the strongest bite of any cat relative to their size, allowing them to pierce turtle shells and caiman skulls. They eat over 85 prey species including deer, peccaries, capybara, fish, caimans, and turtles, often hunting near rivers.
generalKnowledge.what do orcas eat: Orca diet depends on ecotype: resident orcas eat fish (especially salmon), transient orcas hunt marine mammals including seals, sea lions, dolphins, and even other whales, and offshore orcas favor sharks. They are the ocean's apex predators with no natural enemies.
generalKnowledge.what do blue whales eat: Blue whales feed almost exclusively on krill (tiny shrimp-like crustaceans), consuming up to 4 tonnes per day during feeding season. They are lunge feeders, accelerating through dense krill swarms with their mouths open and filtering water through baleen plates.
generalKnowledge.what do manta rays eat: Manta rays are filter feeders that eat plankton, small fish, and krill. They swim slowly through dense patches of prey with their cephalic fins open like a funnel, filtering water through their gill plates. They can consume up to 30 kg of plankton per day.
generalKnowledge.what do hammerhead sharks eat: Hammerhead sharks eat stingrays, fish, octopuses, squid, and crustaceans. Their wide, flattened head (cephalofoil) gives them 360-degree vertical vision and houses a dense array of electroreceptors (ampullae of Lorenzini) that detect rays buried in sand.
generalKnowledge.what do bald eagles eat: Bald eagles are primarily piscivores, diving to snatch fish from near the water's surface with their talons. They also eat waterfowl, small mammals, and frequently steal food from other birds (kleptoparasitism). In winter, they gather at rivers to feed on spawning salmon.
generalKnowledge.what do owls eat: Owls are carnivores that eat small mammals (mice, voles, rabbits), birds, insects, fish, and amphibians depending on the species. They swallow prey whole or in large pieces, then regurgitate compact 'owl pellets' containing indigestible fur, feathers, and bones.
generalKnowledge.what do cobras eat: Cobras are carnivores that eat small mammals, birds, lizards, frogs, eggs, and other snakes — including venomous ones. King cobras specialize almost exclusively in eating other snakes. They kill prey with fast-acting neurotoxic venom, then swallow it whole.
generalKnowledge.what do pythons eat: Pythons are non-venomous constrictors that eat mammals and birds. Reticulated pythons — the world's longest snake — can swallow deer, pigs, and sun bears whole. They kill by coiling around prey and suffocating it, then consume it head-first.
generalKnowledge.what do anacondas eat: Green anacondas are aquatic constrictors that eat fish, birds, caimans, capybaras, deer, and even jaguars in rare cases. They ambush prey at the water's edge, constrict it, and swallow it whole — their jaws stretch to accommodate enormous prey. After a large meal they may not eat for months.
generalKnowledge.what do octopuses eat: Octopuses are carnivores that eat crabs, lobsters, shrimp, clams, fish, and other mollusks. They use their arms to pry open shells, inject venom to paralyze prey, and drill through shells with their hard beak. They are active hunters with excellent vision and problem-solving ability.
generalKnowledge.what do komodo dragons eat: Komodo dragons are apex predators that eat deer, pigs, goats, water buffalo, and carrion. They kill with a combination of serrated teeth, venom (which prevents blood clotting), and a bite that delivers shock-inducing trauma. They can consume up to 80% of their body weight in a single feeding.

### The Amazon Rainforest

The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, covering approximately **5.5 million km²** across 9 countries (primarily Brazil, Peru, Colombia).

**Key statistics:**
- Produces ~20% of the world's oxygen (though it also consumes ~20% — net contribution is debated)
- Contains ~10% of all species on Earth

- The Amazon River discharges ~20% of all freshwater entering the world's oceans
- Inhabited by ~30 million people, including ~400 indigenous tribes (some uncontacted)

**Deforestation crisis:**
- ~17% of the Amazon has been deforested since the 1970s

- Deforestation releases stored carbon: Brazilian Amazon emitted more CO₂ than it absorbed in 2021
